title: Part 1
text: Chapter 1: Conductive Reasoning The second ring of the facility was unusually quiet — just the low, rhythmic hum of overhead fluorescents and the faint echo of someone vaulting something three rooms over. Herman didn’t care. He had more pressing problems. Namely, the flailing cop draped over one shoulder, and the freshly sabotaged hook directly in his path. The hook had clattered to the ground just as the Doctor rounded the corner, Leon kicking and struggling wildly on his shoulder. He had finally started to come around fully from the baton strike that set him prone and was now well on his way to breaking Herman's grip on his waistline. Jake had just finished dismantling it — fast fingers, smug grin — and the nuisance flipped Herman off before vanishing down a side hallway, feet barely touching the tile, content to make the Doctor's job as difficult as physically possible. “Great,” Herman muttered, voice thick with irritation and exhaustion. “Just great.” Herman exhaled slowly through his teeth and adjusted his grip as Leon squirmed again, staggering slightly to the side as a knee almost hit his head, and surveyed the area. The next closest hook was too far off, and the basement with its indestructible hook quartet was clearly out of range. But this particular survivor was one of those. Not fast. Not loud. Not even slippery. Just — gone, the second he got loose. A ghost in denim and bruises. He did not have the patience to track him down yet again before the gates could release him back to the Fog. The Entity was annoyed enough with how often survivors escaped lately. It wouldn't serve him to let this one loose in the halls. Herman ripped Leon, still flailing, from his shoulder and threw him at a locker. He hit the edge of the wood with a sharp crack, the impact knocking the wind from him and kicking the door open to catch him a second time on the way down. Dazed, Leon rolled onto his back, trying to refocus his eyes before finding himself being hoisted up again. "Nothing personal, Mr. Kennedy. I would have preferred to use a basement hook and be done with this chase. But you seem particularly animated today and I am not in the mood to roll an ankle on the steps with your wriggling about." He navigated into a nearby room, dumping Leon heavily against the cabinets on one wall. Old carts littered the space — rusted gurneys with half-locked wheels, trays with upturned pans, a few overturned IV poles resting like skeletal limbs along the walls. The air stank faintly of dust and ozone, like a place struck by lightning long ago and left to rot. It would serve perfectly to keep this particular migraine contained for the time being, he mused to himself as he crouched to rummage through the pouches at the man’s waist. The pest always had some kind of random item on hand that the Entity hadn't deemed important enough to remove; and sure enough, in one of the stained and battered hip pouches, he found a set of bright silver handcuffs. These soldier types were always so predictable. Real steel, not prop bullshit. The Entity must’ve let them pass without flagging their intent. Or maybe she just liked what they could do when repurposed. "You have a nasty habit of vanishing into the dust when I stop looking, and I have a quota to fill today. Therefore, you are going to wait right here until I can locate your little saboteur friend and ensure that he can no longer disable the tools I require to do my job." A painful wrenching tug on his shoulder to pull him to his feet, and a sharp click, and Leon was secured to a padlocked cabinet by one wrist. He winced against the strain on his shoulder, pulling himself into a heavy lean against the cabinet and trying to shake off the gray at the edges of his vision from the earlier impact. Herman frowned slightly at the glassy expression in Leon's eyes and briefly touched his baton to the cabinet. CRACK . The charge arced through the cabinet and into the cuff in an instant. Leon jolted — back arching, breath catching in his throat like it had been yanked by force. A small sound escaped him — half growl, half gasp — and then he sagged again, panting. Wide-eyed. Awake. Much better. "Rise and shine, Mr. Kennedy. The Entity prefers her meals still screaming, afterall. It won't do for you to be too concussed to appreciate her attention, now, would it? Now if you'll excuse me, I have a pest to find. Once I locate him, I'll be sure to bring him here so I can fry him personally at your feet for the grievous insult of interfering with my work. Then we can resume from where we left off. Don't go anywhere, now!" And with that, the Doctor stormed out of the room to continue his hunt, his manic giggle floating down the hallway with the diminishing terror radius, leaving Leon dazed and tugging at his own cuffs as they dug angry red marks into his wrist. He let out a hiss as the motion pulled too fast, too far, the shoulder lighting up in protest. Not dislocated, but close enough to threaten it if he got clever. The wrist burned. It wasn’t the surface sting — he’d felt that before. From tasers, from volts, from the Doctor’s regular blasts — it was deeper . An ache curling through tendon and bone, buzzing in the socket of his shoulder. Leon blinked hard, the afterimage of that electric snap still painting sharp edges behind his eyelids. The world tilted, but settled. "Ok, less than ideal..." Leon twisted at the cuff experimentally. Nothing. No give in the chain, no flex in the cabinet. He patted down pockets, flipping open his pouches and pulling random bits of junk from inside. Small rocks for distracting, pens, an empty pepper spray bottle, spare roll of bandages... nothing particularly useful. More importantly, no keys. Tried the back pocket. His belt loops. Under the radio clip. Still nothing. It seemed Herman had pocketed his cuff keys while searching him. Fantastic. “Of course he did,” Leon muttered under his breath, voice dry. “Why wouldn’t he?” Glancing around the room didn’t offer anything much to help either. Trays stacked in one corner, two overturned gurneys, an IV pole across the floor like a tripping hazard that never got cleaned up. Lots of metal, but anything sharp or sturdy enough to pry with was too far away to test out. He reached out, more careful this time, fingers sweeping what debris was within arm’s length. A toppled tray. The edge of an overturned gurney. Something that might’ve once been a pen but was now too bent to be useful. Not even so much as a staple or paperclip to pick the lock with, not that he had ever been really good at it. That was more Jill's specialty from what the others had told him. "Looks like I'm waiting, then. Damnit. Just had to get the one guy who is willing to improvise." He leaned his head back against the metal, rubbing at his wrenched shoulder with his free hand, and closed his eyes. Just for a second. Just to think. Not like he was going anywhere. The cuff rattled sharply as Leon pulled against the chain, testing for any give. The cabinet creaked, but didn’t budge. “C’mon,” he growled under his breath, planting his boots and bracing into the motion. The metal groaned again, louder this time, but still held firm. Another tug. Another ache in his wrist. Still no movement. In the distance, he could pick up the sounds of the others moving quickly around the building. The Doctor's thudding steps were easy enough to pick up even without the weird aura field that set his heart hammering in his head, and the speed of the smaller scuffing steps told him that a chase was on nearby. Fast. Light. Meg, maybe? Not likely Jake either way. Good. With how annoyed the Doctor was at Jake right now, he might decide to get creative there too. Best to let him take out his frustration on some normal hook kills. Unpleasant, but at least everyone knew what to expect. Sharp stab, a brief moment of terror, then back to the campfire to rest. Not too terrible in the long run. He stilled for a moment, listening. The uneven echo of sprinting feet. The skittering scrape of something being vaulted. Then that familiar electric crackle in the air — a rising static hum that meant only one thing: Herman had eyes on them. The air shifted, sharp and metallic. Leon stiffened. He’d felt that before. The lead-up to one of the Doctor’s area-wide shocks — a burst meant to disorient, slow reaction times, force mistakes. Of course, he would be trying to slow the survivor down, scramble them just enough to confuse movement. It always stung, and everyone had long since learned the taste in the air that preceded it. The shock wave passed easily through the far wall, sparks dancing in white arcs from corner to corner. He followed the flickers with his eyes — arcs of energy crawling across desk legs, chair frames, handles. Everything metal. Metal. His eyes locked on the metal cuff. The realization hit him a breath too late. The shockwave hit the filing cabinet like lightning striking a weathervane. The pain was instant, blinding, slicing through the cuff and across his bones, discharging across flesh and muscle alike. Every nerve lit up like copper wire in a furnace. His scream tangled in his throat as his knees buckled, limbs locking against the intrusion in violent lurches. His hip slammed against the cabinet on the way back to the floor, and for one breathless second, he hung there — suspended by his arm, muscles locked, nerves screaming. He gasped sharply as the chase passed by, then choked on the tail end of it, body twitching as the last of the voltage bled out through him, leaving him gasping and grasping at the cement of the floor as if it could somehow anchor his nerves back in place. He didn’t remember falling. Only the pain. And the taste of metal in the back of his throat. His arm was stretched painfully above him, cuffed wrist still locked to the cabinet. His body had collapsed at an angle — one hip on the floor, the other twisted awkwardly against the base of the unit. His legs shook beneath him, muscles twitching from the aftershock. The room smelled like burnt ozone now. Like the air just after a lightning strike. Leon stayed down for a while, breathing through clenched teeth, trying to will his nerves into compliance. Eventually, the tremors softened enough to let him sit up straighter. Leon pressed his back to the cabinet, breath hitching as he tried to ease the strain from his arm. The muscles in his shoulder burned from the jolt. Every nerve felt skinned raw, still catching echoes of the voltage that had torn through him. His fingers were numb. The cuff bit deep into raw skin. He took another look around the room, a horrified understanding slowly coming to the surface. It wasn’t just cluttered. It was loaded . Metal trays. Surgical carts. Gurneys with chrome legs. Even the cabinet he was chained to had rivets and handles begging to carry current. Every piece of furniture in here had a conductive surface. The static had nowhere else to go but through the one organic thing grounded in the room. And this room? It was in the middle of everything . He knew this layout well. There were at least three generators within range of this hallway. Half the damned trial route ran straight past this door. And every time Herman used his static field to slow someone down, the blast would pass through the walls, seek out the nearest conductors... And arc right into him . Not on purpose. Not even malicious. Just... collateral. Leon stared up at his cuffed wrist. The skin was already red, edges ringed with angry indentations. The others had no idea. Oh God. Every single time they passed through in chase... it would happen again . They would have no choice but to keep coming back. And he would have no choice but to keep taking it. “.... Shit.” Chapter 2: Short Circuit Jake crouched low behind a cracked vinyl privacy screen, its peeling edge pressed against his shoulder as he tried to stay perfectly still. The footsteps were close — not quite sprinting, but fast enough to signal active chase. Somewhere nearby, a generator had blown — he’d heard it not long ago, a sharp burst and the whine of overtaxed wires. The hallway had lit briefly with the hum of a static surge. A wide-area pulse. The jolt had dropped him into a dream of white noise and warped faces — the floor writhing beneath him like something alive, muscles twitching out of sequence for minutes after. He’d woken up behind a generator he didn’t remember fixing, pulse hammering in time with a memory he couldn’t name. He wasn’t keen on doing that again anytime soon. He pressed one hand to the floor to steady himself, heart beating too loud in his ears. He felt it in his teeth before he felt it in his skin — the telltale buzz of an incoming shock. It gathered pressure like a weather front, a phantom weight that prickled across the back of his neck and tightened the tendons in his forearms. It felt fainter than the last few times he had been shocked today. Hopefully, he was far enough out of range to not get more than a passing numbness this time. It was never overly debilitating, but the random hallucinations and muscle twinges were something he could really do without. He flexed his fingers, checking for tremors. Still there — faint, but present. Just enough to make clipping a wire a pain in the ass. “Just once,” he muttered to himself, “I’d like to have a normal goddamn trial without getting brain-fried before I even find a teammate.” From somewhere down the hall came a startled cry — high-pitched, unmistakably Meg — and Jake tensed, waiting for the telltale thud of a hit or the snap of a pallet drop. Either one would let him know what direction they were looping in so he wouldn’t have to come out of hiding so soon. No point getting zapped for a moral support cameo. He’d seen her tank worse hits and walk it off. And if it was just a standard burst, she’d be fine. Shaken, maybe, but still mobile. The air buzzed again with a second charge building. Jake barely had time to suck in a breath before something new reached his ears — a voice, muffled, but urgent enough to raise every hair on his neck. "Wait - DON’T..." The shockwave rippled through the air, a low static buzz that flared briefly across the space. A single spark cracked off the edge of the privacy screen, catching Jake on the arm. He let out a sharp hiss, jerking away from the contact. “Damn it—” he muttered, rubbing the angry red mark where the spark had connected with skin. The scream that followed made him pause in confusion. It had layers — a secondary pitch, deeper, more ragged. Not fear. Not panic. Just raw pain. Jake’s brow furrowed. That wasn’t Meg. Someone else had gotten caught in the blast. If he didn’t know better, he’d think someone got hit trying to talk Herman down or something. Unless you were right up against it, the shocks only messed with your mind and nerves. They didn’t really hurt . For someone to sound like they were in that much pain from a static blast, they would have needed to be practically touching the Doctor. Who else was with them, anyways? He remembered Herman carrying someone when he’d pulled that earlier sabotage, but hadn’t gotten a good look. Whoever it was hadn’t been screaming at the time — just flailing — so he’d assumed they’d sort themselves out or recover once the hook was back. Regardless, it would have been a stupid move, really. The Doctor wasn’t one of the killers who could be reasoned with. He took his job seriously and with a delight that bordered on mania some days. But that second scream — that yelp — landed wrong. It didn’t echo forward. It set the hairs on the back of Jake’s neck prickling, an unease sitting heavy in his stomach. It had sounded like it came from behind the wall at his back. The room at his back didn’t have a generator in it. No totem. No chest. Nothing useful. Just junk furniture, broken trays, the kind of clutter the Fog dumped in rooms to fill space. He’d passed through it earlier with barely a glance. It wasn’t even a particularly good hiding spot. So why the hell would anyone be in there? Did something get added in that he missed? The chaos outside eventually pulled away, the chase bleeding into another corner of the complex. Jake stood slowly, ears straining, and caught the tail end of a broken voice, exhausted and angry, from behind the wall. “Fucking hell. Can I just — breathe — for two seconds?” Jake’s brow furrowed. He placed a palm against the cool tile, tracing his way silently around the corner until he reached the doorframe of the adjacent room. Eyes scanning instinctively. Still no objectives. Still nothing but overturned carts and scattered debris. Which made the figure slumped against the far cabinet in a battered mess of RPD blue even more out of place. Jake whistled low under his breath and stepped in, eyes scanning the setup. Leon was cuffed at the wrist — arm stretched uncomfortably above his head, body half-curled beneath it like he’d dropped mid-spasm. His shoulder looked angry. Raw tension threaded through the entire arm. “Jesus, man,” Jake muttered. “You look like shit.” Leon grunted in response, shifting his weight to pull himself off the floor, leaning heavily against the cabinet as he tried taking the weight off his shoulder. “Don’t sugarcoat it.” Jake crossed the room in three strides, crouching to examine the cuff. “What the hell happened to you?” Leon exhaled a humorless laugh and rattled the cuff lightly. “Apparently, my hiding skills got me promoted from gen jockey. Welcome to my new desk job.” Jake tugged at the metal, bracing one foot on the cabinet as he tried to get the chain to snap. It creaked lightly against the cabinet handle, but didn’t budge. “You’ve gotta be kidding me. He cuffed you to a freaking filing cabinet?” “Didn’t even get a chair. The working conditions here suck.” “Don’t you guys usually have keys for these things?” Leon pushed his bangs back with one hand, yanking the cuff sharply in irritation and wincing as it bit into him again. “Pretty sure the Doctor pocketed them while he was searching me. I was a little... out of it. ” He gestured vaguely toward the wall with his free hand. “Didn’t exactly get the luxury of staying conscious through most of the decision-making process.” Jake huffed through his nose. “Well, that’s comforting.” He reached for the screwdriver clipped to his belt and wedged the flat end into the hinge between the cuff and the cabinet. The metal resisted, but he leaned in harder, tongue between his teeth, working the angle. It wasn’t the cleanest method, but maybe if he could just pry the lip— Leon’s body jerked suddenly beside him. “Hold on — don’t—” The air had shifted again — that metallic taste returned — and in the moment, Jake had completely missed it. Leon surged forward, shoving Jake back with his free just as the cabinet lit up like a bug zapper. Electricity danced along the edges, funnelled straight through the cuff and into Leon’s arm. He arched violently, mouth open in a scream that caught midway, choking on itself as his body seized and bucked against the restraint. Jake hit the floor with a hard thud, palms scraping against the tile. His screwdriver skittered off to the side, spinning once before vanishing beneath a rusted gurney. “ Shit— ” He twisted, scrambling to push upright just in time to see Leon slam against the cabinet, back arching, head snapping back. The sparks died off, and for a moment, all Jake could do was stare. Leon sagged forward, the cuff dragging taut as he crumpled, then steadied himself with one trembling arm. His eyes were open — unfocused, distant, breath caught somewhere between a gasp and a choke. One hand curled against his vest, nails biting fabric as he struggled to ride out the recoil. “Leon?” No answer. Jake took a step forward. Leon lifted a shaky hand — not up, but out. Just a small wave. A breathless “wait.” A hold. Jake froze. Leon knelt fully, head bowed, breathing shallow and quick. His shoulders rocked faintly with the rhythm of his pulse. After a few moments, he dropped back against the cabinet again, letting the cuff yank taut above him with a hiss. “...What the fuck was that?” Jake asked, quieter now. Almost like the walls might answer. Jake’s eyes traced the line between Leon’s arm and the cuffs, up through the metal cabinet, and around the room. Sparks still popped gently between pieces of furniture across the room, like static creeping along a thundercloud’s edge. Jake followed the line — from one overturned tray to a chrome IV stand, then up the cabinet where Leon’s arm trembled just shy of collapse. “Holy shit, it’s focusing the static blasts, isn’t it?” “Yeah,” Leon rasped, settling himself off his knees and sitting back against the cabinet, “Yeah, I may have noticed.” “You were trying to tell the others not to bring the chase down this way. That’s what I heard earlier.” Leon’s head thunked against the cabinet as he panted. “It’d be nice if I could get a warning out before the world goes white again. They’re moving around so fast... there’s no time.” “There’re easily 3 generators within radius of here, too. Fucking hell...” Leon nodded, eyes distant. Jake was catching up fast, drawing the same conclusion. Even if they managed to warn the others off, eventually they would HAVE to come back this way. There was simply no avoiding it. Jake idly fiddled with his toolbelt, trying to think of a plan. “There’s gotta be a way to break this.” He crouched beside the cuff again, eyeing the hinge. “I’ve pried a lock off a hook tower before. This is just... smaller.” He flexed his hand, already tingling from the earlier zap. “If I had something better than a screwdriver—” His breath caught. The hook. His mind skipped back — to the moment in the hallway. The sabotaged hook. The thrashing figure on Herman’s shoulder. He hadn’t known who it was. Hadn’t stopped to check. “ Fuck, ” Jake whispered. “That was you. I—” He stood up fast, hands bracing on his head. “If I hadn’t—shit—if I hadn’t taken that hook down—” Leon waved him off dismissively. “Don’t waste time feeling bad about something that worked. It slowed him down, gave you space. He just got creative. Guilt won’t help us now.” “...But —" “It was the right call in the moment. Seriously. I would have done the same. What we need now is some way to break these off.” Jake swallowed the guilt back and tried to focus. He was right. It wasn’t serving anyone right now. He could warn the others to avoid the hallway for now, but they would eventually run out of further generators to work on, and most of the good loops and escape routes came straight through the area. Even if they managed to get it all done, there was no way for Leon to get out of the end gate short of breaking those stupid cuffs off, or else wait for Herman to send him back through the Fog the old-fashioned way. And with how badly those static blasts were being focused and funneled through the furniture, there was no guarantee what shape he’d even be in at that point. So, it would have to be a tool hunt, then. Though with all the random toolboxes in this place that he had found over the trials, Jake had never once seen something actually USEFUL for something like this. No crowbars. No wire cutters. Not even a broken scalpel. The Entity didn’t leave them with what they needed. Just what she thought might be entertaining. “Of course she wouldn’t,” he muttered. “Not her style. Flashlights that barely work, medkits that run out before you stop bleeding, but the second you need something practical— ” Both men seemed to come to the same conclusion, shared across a look. They needed the keys. Jake looked at the door. Then at Leon. “I’ll find them.” Leon managed a faint smirk — but it faded quickly, buried under the tension winding back into his shoulders. He nodded, closed his eyes, and waited for the air to shift again, tracking Jake’s footfalls until they faded down the hallway. Chapter 3: Conductive Reasoning Jake had stopped checking his surroundings three drawers ago. Probably not the best call, all things considered. But after the fifth tray of shattered glass and bent syringes, the paranoia had dulled into background noise. Every cabinet, cart, and table in this wing had offered nothing but rusted scalpels, cracked syringes, and bandage rolls that looked like they’d been soaked in something before the Fog found them. It wasn’t even creepy anymore. Just tedious. Nothing had jumped him yet, and if Herman was still busy lighting up the far end of the map, that bought him time. Not comfort. Just time. He slammed another drawer shut, the metal shrieking in protest, and ripped open the next one. More gauze. Rusted scalpels tangled like brittle weeds. A blood pressure cuff half-melted to the lining. “ They’re just keys, ” he muttered, rifling with increasing irritation. “How hard is it to find a set of fucking keys? What are they, an inch wide? Half an inch? What, do they disintegrate if you make eye contact with them?” The next drawer had old notebooks — pages torn and curling with moisture, most of the ink blurred beyond recognition. He flipped one open on reflex. Mold across the spine. The few pages still intact were stained with dark splashes that could’ve been ink. Could’ve been blood. Hard to tell anymore. Everything the Fog touched decayed in stages. Wood splintered. Paper decayed. Even metal rusted faster than it had any right to. He tossed it aside and turned to the next tray when a scream knifed through the walls. He froze. One clean rip of pain, sharp enough to echo down through the vents. He crouched instinctively, angling himself toward the hallway’s edge and holding still. Leon. The lights above him buzzed faintly, a flicker of static skipping down the line like a warning. No footsteps followed. No voices. Just the distant groan of the building settling in its chains, and the faint crackle of static in the overhead lights. Jake exhaled slow through his nose, grounding himself with a palm against the floor. A single jolt like that wasn’t part of a chase. That meant Herman was still near Leon — and nowhere near here. He rubbed a hand down his face and stood. If Leon was still screaming, it meant he was still alive. If he was alive, Jake still had time. And he wasn’t wasting it. Jake spotted Meg two rooms over, crouched beside a battered generator that was audibly wheezing under the strain of whatever makeshift repairs she was forcing on it. Her sleeves were rolled up past her elbows, grease smudged along one cheek, fingers working fast inside the open panel. She didn’t even look up. He approached slowly, boots scuffing tile just loud enough to not startle — or so he thought. The second his hand touched her shoulder, she jolted like he’d set her on fire. “Shit—!” Meg yelped, slapping a live wire aside just before it could spark against the casing. “ What?! What could you POSSIBLY want that needs scaring a person so bad?!” Jake held up both hands, voice low. “We have a problem.” Meg glared, but stilled. “The Doctor has Leon locked down in one of the rooms near the main gen cluster,” he said quietly. “I need you to stay clear of that entire side of the building.” She blinked once, then rolled her eyes and dove back into the wires. “You’d have me leave that bastard a perfect patrol path when we’re this close to done?” she snapped, voice curt. “I don’t think so. We need at least one — maybe two — of those gens online or we’re never getting the gate. I’m headed that way as soon as I’m done here. You should be too. ” “No, Meg. You don’t get it. ” Jake took a step closer, lowering his voice. “Leon’s over there getting wrecked by static every time someone runs past. You need to stay the hell away.” “He knows what he signed up for,” Meg muttered, not looking at him. “He’ll live. Guy’s tough as nails. I think he’ll forgive a few shocks and a little panic if it gets the doors open faster.” Jake grit his teeth. “Meg, he’s cuffed to the furniture . He can’t leave the blast radius.” That stopped her. Meg set her tools down, eyes hard. “The shocks
